name: Acid-Base II Case Chains
intro: Twenty-one patients, most with more than one process at once. Read the pH, match the carbon dioxide and bicarbonate to it, calculate and albumin-correct the anion gap, check compensation (Winter formula, the acute and chronic ratios), compare the change in anion gap with the change in bicarbonate, then name what fits the patient. Every value comes with its normal range.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.vignette: A 71-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit with a severe urinary tract infection that has spread to her blood (sepsis). She is confused, warm and breathing fast. Her blood lactate is high. She has no kidney disease, no diarrhea or vomiting, no diabetes, and has taken no toxins.

steps.label: pH
steps.prompt: What does the pH show?

options.e: A pH below 6.7 or above 7.6 is unsustainable. A pH of 7.40 is well inside those limits, and in fact normal. Tell: unsustainable marks how far the pH has moved, not which way.
Acidemia means a pH below 7.35. This pH of 7.40 is inside 7.35 to 7.45, so it is a normal pH. Tell: below the range is acidemia, above it is alkalemia.

Correct. The pH of 7.40 sits inside 7.35 to 7.45. A normal pH does not rule out an acid-base problem: an acidosis and an alkalosis can pull against each other and leave the pH in the middle, so the carbon dioxide and bicarbonate still have to be read.
Alkalemia means a pH above 7.45. This pH of 7.40 is inside 7.35 to 7.45, so it is a normal pH. Tell: below the range is acidemia, above it is alkalemia.

walk: Compare the pH with its normal range, 7.35 to 7.45.
So: a normal pH. A normal pH can still hide a mixed disorder, so keep reading.

steps.label: Normal pH?
steps.prompt: The pH is normal. What do these values show?

options.e: Compensation never fully corrects the pH in a simple disorder; it only brings it closer to normal. So a normal pH of 7.40 is never a simple disorder that compensated all the way. Tell: a normal pH with abnormal values means two processes pulling against each other.

A normal pH does not rule out an acid-base problem. Here the carbon dioxide and bicarbonate are out of range, so something is moving them. Tell: look at the pH, the carbon dioxide and the bicarbonate before calling it normal.

Correct. The pH of 7.40 is normal, but the carbon dioxide of 20 is below 35, which raises the pH; the bicarbonate of 12 is below 22, which lowers the pH. Each would move the pH a different way, a tug of war that leaves it in the middle. Compensation never fully corrects the pH, so a normal pH with abnormal values means a mixed disorder.

There can never be more than one primary respiratory disorder: a patient cannot breathe too fast and too slow at once. Only one process can come from the carbon dioxide; the other must be metabolic. Tell: one respiratory process at most, metabolic ones can stack.

walk: Abnormal values with a normal pH: each pulls the pH a different way, and compensation alone never returns the pH fully to normal.

steps.label: Two processes
steps.prompt: Read the carbon dioxide and bicarbonate on their own. Which two processes are present?

options.e: A respiratory acidosis needs a high carbon dioxide, and this one is 20. Here the carbon dioxide of 20 is below 35: a respiratory alkalosis, and the bicarbonate of 12 is below 22: a metabolic acidosis. Tell: each value names its own process; read the direction of each.

A metabolic alkalosis needs a high bicarbonate, and this one is 12; a respiratory acidosis needs a high carbon dioxide, and this one is 20. Here the carbon dioxide of 20 is below 35: a respiratory alkalosis, and the bicarbonate of 12 is below 22: a metabolic acidosis. Tell: each value names its own process; read the direction of each.

A metabolic alkalosis needs a high bicarbonate, and this one is 12. Here the carbon dioxide of 20 is below 35: a respiratory alkalosis, and the bicarbonate of 12 is below 22: a metabolic acidosis. Tell: each value names its own process; read the direction of each.

Correct. Read each value on its own: the carbon dioxide of 20 is below 35: a respiratory alkalosis, and the bicarbonate of 12 is below 22: a metabolic acidosis. One respiratory and one metabolic process can run together. They pull the pH opposite ways, so it ends up normal.

walk: Carbon dioxide 20 (normal 35 to 45): low, so respiratory alkalosis.
Bicarbonate 12 (normal 22 to 26): low, so metabolic acidosis.
Only one respiratory process is possible at a time; a metabolic one can join it.
So: metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis.

steps.label: Anion gap
steps.prompt: Calculate the anion gap.

options.e: Correct. Anion gap = sodium - (bicarbonate + chloride) = 138 - (12 + 104) = 138 - 116 = 22. The normal gap is 6 to 12, about 10 on average.
26.2 adds the potassium of 4.2. The formula has no potassium: 138 - (12 + 104) = 22. Tell: sodium, bicarbonate and chloride are the only three values.
34 is sodium minus chloride only (138 - 104); the bicarbonate was left out. Both measured anions come off the sodium: 138 - (12 + 104) = 22. Tell: add bicarbonate and chloride first, then subtract.
46 adds the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it (138 - 104 + 12). The gap takes away bicarbonate and chloride together: 138 - 116 = 22. Tell: the parentheses hold bicarbonate plus chloride.

steps.label: Reading the gap
steps.prompt: How should this anion gap be read?

options.e: Correct. The gap of 22 is above the normal 6 to 12, so it is elevated: added unmeasured anions such as ketoacids or lactate. A large gap points to a metabolic acidosis, never a respiratory disorder alone.
A decreased gap is below 6, most often from a low albumin that has not been corrected. The gap of 22 is above 12. Tell: only a gap below 6 is decreased.
The gap is corrected only when albumin is abnormal, and this albumin of 4.6 g/dL is not low. So the gap of 22 is read as it stands. Tell: correct the gap only for an abnormal albumin.
A normal gap is 6 to 12, about 10 on average, and this gap of 22 is above it. Tell: above 12 is elevated, pointing to the increased-gap list.

steps.label: Winter formula
steps.prompt: Use the Winter formula: what carbon dioxide range is expected?

options.e: 8 to 12 mm Hg subtracts the 8 instead of adding it (1.5 x 12 - 8 = 10). The formula adds: 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26, so 24 to 28. Tell: the constant is plus 8.
18 to 22 mm Hg adds 8 to the bicarbonate without multiplying by 1.5 (12 + 8 = 20). The formula is 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26, so 24 to 28. Tell: multiply by 1.5 first, then add 8.
Correct. Winter formula: expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 18 + 8 = 26, plus or minus 2, so 24 to 28 mm Hg. Only the measured bicarbonate goes into it.
30 to 34 mm Hg multiplies the bicarbonate by 2 instead of 1.5 (2 x 12 + 8 = 32). The multiplier is 1.5: 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26, so 24 to 28. Tell: one and a half times the bicarbonate, plus 8.

walk: Winter formula: expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x bicarbonate + 8, plus or minus 2.

steps.label: Compensation check
steps.prompt: Compare the measured carbon dioxide with that range. What does it show?

options.e: A concurrent respiratory acidosis shows as a carbon dioxide above the Winter range. The measured 20 is below the expected 24 to 28. Tell: above the range is respiratory acidosis, below it respiratory alkalosis.

A metabolic acidosis is compensated by the lungs, through carbon dioxide; the kidneys compensate respiratory disorders. The carbon dioxide of 20 is the respiratory side, and it sits below the expected 24 to 28. Tell: a metabolic problem gets a respiratory response.
Correct. The measured carbon dioxide of 20 is below the expected 24 to 28 mm Hg: the lungs are blowing off more than compensation needs, a concurrent respiratory alkalosis.

Metabolic acidosis only means the carbon dioxide sits inside the expected 24 to 28 mm Hg. The measured 20 is below it, so the lungs are not simply compensating. Tell: outside the Winter range means a second, respiratory, process.

walk: Expected carbon dioxide by the Winter formula: 24 to 28 mm Hg.
20 is below the range: inside = metabolic acidosis only; above = concurrent respiratory acidosis; below = concurrent respiratory alkalosis.

steps.label: Gap against bicarbonate
steps.prompt: Compare the change in anion gap with the change in bicarbonate. What does it show?

options.e: The chloride is checked when the gap change is smaller than the bicarbonate change. Here 12 is about equal to 13. Tell: check the chloride only when the bicarbonate fell more than the gap rose.

The change in gap against the change in bicarbonate looks only for other metabolic processes; a respiratory one is found by comparing the carbon dioxide with the expected compensation. Here the gap change is 12 and the bicarbonate change 13. Tell: this comparison is metabolic against metabolic.

Correct. The gap rose 12 (22 - 10) and the bicarbonate fell 13 (25 - 12): about equal, so the added acid explains the whole fall in bicarbonate. A metabolic acidosis only, with no hidden metabolic process.
A concurrent metabolic alkalosis shows as a gap change larger than the bicarbonate change. Here 12 is about equal to 13. Tell: gap change bigger means a hidden alkalosis.

walk: Equal: metabolic acidosis only. Gap change larger: concurrent metabolic alkalosis (seen only with a high gap). Gap change smaller: check the change in chloride.
12 is about equal to 13, so: metabolic acidosis only.

steps.label: What fits
steps.prompt: Which condition best fits this patient and these values?

options.e: Uremia with vomiting is the metabolic acidosis plus metabolic alkalosis pair, and she has no kidney disease or vomiting; her gap change matched her bicarbonate change. Tell: her second process is respiratory.

Diarrhea with lactic acidosis is an increased-gap plus normal-gap pair, and she has no diarrhea; her chloride of 104 is normal. Tell: the low carbon dioxide below the Winter range is the second process.

Correct. Sepsis with lactic acidosis is the classic metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis: lactate raises the gap (22) while her fast breathing drives the carbon dioxide below the Winter range. Her high lactate and infection fit.

Lactic acidosis is one of her processes, but alone it would leave the carbon dioxide inside the Winter range and the pH low. Hers is 20, below 24 to 28, with a normal pH. Tell: two processes, not one.

walk: Processes found: an increased-gap metabolic acidosis (gap 22) and a respiratory alkalosis (carbon dioxide 20, below the Winter range of 24 to 28).
Does the clinical picture fit? Sepsis with a high lactate, breathing fast.
